## Importing and visualising EEG data

In this vignette, we illustrate how to analyse one-dimensional EEG time series using Bayesian generalised additive multilevel models (BGAMMs). We use an example dataset from the [`eegkit` package](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=eegkit), containing event-related potentials (ERPs) recorded from multiple participants, channels, and experimental groups. First, we import the data and visualise the average ERP waveforms across groups for a selection of channels.

```{r data-import, fig.width = 12, fig.height = 12}
library(neurogam)
library(ggplot2)
library(eegkit)
library(dplyr)

# Change default brms backend
options(brms.backend = "cmdstanr")

# Use the ggplot2 neurogam theme
theme_set(theme_neurogam() )

# Import eegdata
data("eegdata", package = "eegkitdata")

# plotting the average ERP per group and some channels
eegdata |>
    summarise(voltage = mean(voltage), .by = c(group, channel, time) ) |>
    filter(channel %in% sample(x = unique(levels(eegdata$channel) ), size = 9) ) |> 
    ggplot(aes(x = time, y = voltage, colour = group) ) +
    geom_line() +
    facet_wrap(~channel)
```

For simplicity, we focus on a single channel (`P6`), convert time to seconds, round numerical values, and remove missing observations.

```{r data-reshape}
# reshape the data
eeg_data <- eegdata |>
    # keeping only one channel
    dplyr::filter(channel == "P6") |>
    # converting timesteps to seconds
    mutate(time = (time + 1) / 256) |>
    # rounding numeric variables
    mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 4) ) ) |>
    # removing NAs
    na.omit()

# show a few rows
head(eeg_data)
```

## Fitting the model

We first fit a BGAMM to assess differences between experimental groups over time. The model estimates smooth temporal trajectories while accounting for participant-level variability. Statistical evidence is assessed using posterior odds, with a threshold of 10.

```{r clusters, results = "hide"}
# fitting the BGAMM to identify clusters (around 30 min on 4 parallel apple M4 cores)
results <- testing_through_time(
    # EEG data
    data = eeg_data,
    # participant column
    participant_id = "subject",
    # EEG column
    outcome_id = "voltage",
    # name of predictor in data
    predictor_id = "group",
    # basis dimension
    kvalue = 20,
    # baseline period
    baseline_window = c(0, 0.1),
    # we recommend fitting the GAMM on summary statistics (mean and SD)
    multilevel = "summary",
    # threshold on posterior odds
    threshold = 10,
    # participant-specific smooth?
    varying_smooth = TRUE,
    # number of MCMCs
    chains = 4,
    # number of parallel cores
    cores = 4,
    # save the model
    file = "cache/temporal_model"
    )
```

```{r clusters2, eval = FALSE, echo = FALSE, results = "hide"}
# load the model
previous_model <- readRDS(file = "cache/temporal_model.rds")

results <- testing_through_time(
    # EEG data
    data = eeg_data,
    # reuse previous model
    previous_model = previous_model,
    # participant column
    participant_id = "subject",
    # EEG column
    outcome_id = "voltage",
    # name of predictor in data
    predictor_id = "group",
    # basis dimension
    kvalue = 20,
    # baseline period
    baseline_window = c(0, 0.1),
    # we recommend fitting the GAMM on summary statistics (mean and SD)
    multilevel = "summary",
    # threshold on posterior odds
    threshold = 3,
    # participant-specific smooth?
    varying_smooth = TRUE,
    # number of MCMCs
    chains = 4,
    # number of parallel cores
    cores = 4,
    # save the model
    file = "cache/temporal_model"
    )
```

### Visualising the results

The `print()` method summarises the identified temporal clusters, whereas `plot()` displays the observed data, posterior predictions, and clusters supported by the specified posterior odds threshold.

```{r print-clusters}
# displaying the identified clusters
print(results)
```

```{r clusters-plot, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 6}
# plotting the data, model's predictions, and clusters
plot(results)
```

### Computing clusters at the participant-level

We can also identify temporal clusters separately for each participant. Here, we omit the group predictor (`predictor_id = NA`) and set `participant_clusters = TRUE` to assess when EEG amplitude differs from zero, at both the group and participant levels. Because group membership is constant within participants, the group contrast is not included in this analysis.

```{r clusters-ppt, results = "hide", cache = TRUE}
# fitting the BGAMM to identify clusters
results_ppt <- testing_through_time(
    # EEG data
    data = eeg_data,
    # participant column
    participant_id = "subject",
    # EEG column
    outcome_id = "voltage",
    # baseline period
    baseline_window = c(0, 0.1),
    # here we use no predictor (because group varies across participants)
    predictor_id = NA,
    # group basis dimension
    kvalue = 20,
    # we recommend fitting the GAMM with summary statistics (mean and SD)
    multilevel = "summary",
    # return clusters at both the group and participant levels
    participant_clusters = TRUE,
    # threshold on posterior odds
    threshold = 10,
    # number of MCMCs
    chains = 4,
    # number of parallel cores
    cores = 4
    )
```

### Visualising participant-level results

As before, we can inspect the identified clusters using the dedicated `print()` and `plot()` methods.

```{r print-clusters-ppt}
# displaying the identified clusters
print(results_ppt)
```

```{r clusters-ppt-plot, fig.width = 12, fig.height = 9}
# plotting the data, model's predictions, and clusters
plot(results_ppt)
```

### Posterior predictive checks

Posterior predictive checks (PPCs) help assess how well the model reproduces key features of the observed data. We recommend inspecting model predictions at both the group and participant levels. The `neurogam::ppc()` function provides convenient visualisations, whereas `brms::pp_check()` offers additional diagnostics (see the [bayesplot PPC overview](https://mc-stan.org/bayesplot/reference/PPC-overview.html)).

```{r ppc1-plot, fig.width = 12, fig.height = 6}
# posterior predictive checks (PPCs) at the group level
ppc(object = results, ppc_type = "group")
```

```{r ppc2-plot, fig.width = 12, fig.height = 9}
# posterior predictive checks (PPCs) at the participant level
ppc(object = results, ppc_type = "participant")
```
